scenes.title: Who I am
scenes.narration: My name is Eli Parker. I'm seventeen, a private in a Connecticut regiment of the Continental Army. Back home, I milked cows and split rails on my father's farm. I signed up to fight for liberty. Nobody told me the hardest enemy would be the winter.

scenes.title: Valley Forge
scenes.narration: On the nineteenth of December, we reached a bare, frozen hillside eighteen miles from Philadelphia. There was no town. No barracks. Not even a roof. Just woods and snow, and the ruins of an old iron forge the British had burned. They called the place Valley Forge.

scenes.title: How we got here
scenes.narration: That autumn had gone badly. We lost the fight at Brandywine Creek in September. Two weeks later, the British marched into Philadelphia, our capital, without firing a shot. We struck back at Germantown in October and lost again. Now the British were warm in the city's houses. And we were out here.

scenes.narration: The day before we reached camp, Congress declared a day of Thanksgiving. So we got a special dinner. Each man received half a gill of rice and a tablespoon of vinegar. That was it. That was Thanksgiving. We laughed about it. What else could we do?

scenes.title: Build or freeze
scenes.narration: General Washington gave us an order: build huts, or freeze. Twelve men to a hut, fourteen feet by sixteen, with a fireplace at one end. He offered twelve dollars to the first squad in each regiment to finish. So the whole hillside rang with axes, day and night.

scenes.narration: And here's something I never forgot. The general could have taken a warm farmhouse on the very first night. Instead, he lived in his own canvas tent in the snow, the same as us, while we started on the huts. Men noticed that. I noticed it.

scenes.title: Our hut
scenes.narration: Our hut took us nine days. Logs for the walls. Clay and straw packed into the cracks. Bunks of poles and straw, three high. The chimney was made of sticks and mud, and it caught fire twice. But on the first night with a roof over us nobody said a word. We just slept.

scenes.title: Fire cake
scenes.narration: Food was the worst of it. Most days, there was no meat at all. So we made fire cake. Flour and water, mixed into a paste and baked on a hot stone in the fire. If you asked a man what he had for dinner, he'd say: fire cake and water, sir. Fire cake and water.

scenes.title: No meat!
scenes.narration: Two days after we arrived, a cry started in one hut and spread across the whole camp. No meat! No meat! Thousands of voices in the dark. A surgeon wrote that the valleys echoed it back to us. It wasn't a mutiny. It was hungry men telling the world they were still there.

scenes.title: Barefoot
scenes.narration: Two days before Christmas, General Washington wrote to Congress. He counted two thousand, eight hundred and ninety-eight men in camp who could not do their duty, because they were barefoot, and had almost no clothes. I saw men stand guard on top of their own hats, just to keep their bare feet off the snow.

scenes.title: The smoke
scenes.narration: Inside the huts, the fire kept us alive. But the chimneys pulled badly, and the smoke had nowhere to go. Our eyes were red and running all winter. Twelve men in a room the size of a stable, with wet blankets, smoke, and no fresh air. We didn't know it yet but that was the real danger.

scenes.title: The real enemy
scenes.narration: People think the cold killed us at Valley Forge. It wasn't the cold. It was sickness. Typhus. Dysentery. Pneumonia. They moved through the crowded huts like fire. Before we left that camp, nearly two thousand men had died there. And there was never a battle at Valley Forge. Not one.

scenes.title: Inoculation
scenes.narration: The one sickness we did fight was smallpox. Washington ordered every man who'd never had it to be inoculated. A doctor cut a small scratch in my arm and put a little of the pox into it. I was sick for two weeks. But I never caught the real thing. Two years before, smallpox had wrecked a whole army of ours in Canada.

scenes.title: The starving time
scenes.narration: February was the worst. A thaw turned the roads to deep mud, and the wagons couldn't get through. For days, there was nothing in camp. No meat, no bread, not even flour. Back in December, the general had warned Congress that this army might starve, dissolve, or disperse. In February it nearly did.

scenes.title: Foraging
scenes.narration: Then the general sent foraging parties out across the country to find food, and put General Greene in charge of supplies. They came back with herds of cattle, driven through the snow. When the first cattle walked into camp, men cheered like we'd won a battle. Sam cooked a stew that night. I still remember the smell.

scenes.title: Jonah comes back
scenes.narration: And in March, Jonah walked back into our hut on his own two feet. Thin as a rail, but alive. He sat down by the fire, looked at the stew pot, and said: Is that meat? I haven't laughed like that before or since.

scenes.title: The Prussian
scenes.narration: In March, a stranger began to drill us. A Prussian officer, Baron von Steuben. He barely spoke English. He shouted at us in German and French, and when he ran out of curses, he'd turn to his aide and say: come and swear at them for me in English! We laughed. But we listened.

scenes.title: One army
scenes.narration: Before him, every regiment marched its own way. He gave us one way. How to load faster. How to march in a column and swing into a line. How to use the bayonet instead of running. By May, we weren't thirteen states' worth of farmers anymore. We were one army.

scenes.title: Spring
scenes.narration: Spring came slowly. The snow melted, the mud dried, and the creek ran fast again. Wagons got through. New uniforms came in. Somebody's wife sent a whole crate of stockings. I got my first real pair of shoes since the autumn. I put them on and walked around the hut three times, just to feel it.

scenes.title: The news from France
scenes.narration: On the sixth of May, the news came. France had joined the war on our side. The whole army lined up on the parade ground, and fired a running salute, one musket after another, all the way down the line and back. Thirteen cannon. An extra ration of rum. And for the first time we cheered as winners.

scenes.title: Marching out
scenes.narration: On the nineteenth of June, six months to the day after we arrived, we marched out of Valley Forge. Behind us, the hillside was a field of empty huts. Nine days later, at Monmouth, we met the British in the open field and this time, they did not run us off it.

scenes.title: The empty hut
scenes.narration: Before we left, I went back inside our hut one last time. The fireplace was cold. Somebody had carved twelve names into the logs by the door. Jonah's was there. And Sam's. And mine.

scenes.title: How we survived
scenes.narration: So how did we survive Valley Forge? Huts we built with our own hands. Fire cake and water. Shoes made of raw hide. Friends who sat with you through the fever. And a stubborn idea: that if we just held on until spring, we could still win. And we did.

scenes.title: What comes next
scenes.narration: A hundred and sixty-seven years later, in another December, another American army was trapped in the snow. Christmas, nineteen forty-four, in the frozen forests of Belgium, at a town called Bastogne. Surrounded, outnumbered, and out of almost everything. How did they hold? That story is next.
